column4: Restrictions on buying US dollars and moving money abroad. It protects reserves in the short run, but widens the gap with the parallel dollar, scares off investment and feeds the black market.

column3: Central bank financing of the Treasury
column4: The central bank prints pesos to finance the deficit. It is quick money, but it is the classic source of Argentine inflation: it weakens the currency and erodes wages and pensions.
A tax on farm exports, mainly soybeans. It raises a lot of money and makes food cheaper, but farmers fiercely oppose it and it discourages exports, which costs dollars.
A surcharge on buying dollars, plane tickets and spending abroad. It raises revenue and curbs demand for foreign currency, but hits the middle class and widens the exchange-rate gap.

An agreement with the International Monetary Fund: disbursements and backing in exchange for targets on the deficit, money printing and reserves. It calms markets but is unpopular with much of the country.
Price agreements and freezes in supermarkets. They slow inflation for a few months, but cause shortages, a black market and a rebound when lifted.
Decades-long tax, customs and currency benefits for projects over two hundred million dollars in energy, mining and infrastructure.
Public investment and pipelines to exploit the world's second-largest shale gas reserve. It can turn around the energy balance and bring in dollars, at an environmental cost.
Promotion of lithium mining in the Puna highlands. It attracts investment and exports, but worries local communities and environmentalists about water use.
Money the national government hands to governors outside the federal tax-sharing scheme. It buys support in Congress and stability, but encourages patronage.
The state pays part of electricity and gas bills. It helps households and holds down inflation, but it costs a fortune, discourages saving and investment and ends in blackouts.
Cheap bus and train fares paid with national funds, concentrated in Greater Buenos Aires. They help workers, but the provinces complain.
Lets people retire without the full years of contributions, mostly women and informal workers. It expands coverage, but strains the system.
The formula that updates pensions. If it lags inflation, pensioners lose; if it is generous, spending soars.
Work-for-welfare and cash programs partly run by grassroots organisations. They hold down extreme poverty and unrest, but have a poor image among the middle class.

Federal forces clear street and road blockades without a court order. It restores traffic and pleases part of the middle class, but clashes with unions, grassroots groups and human rights organisations.
Changes to the employment contract law: severance pay, probation periods and company-level agreements. Employers have asked for it for decades; the unions see it as a red line.
Compulsory union dues and union control of health insurance funds. It sustains the power of the labour federation, which in return grants or withholds social peace.
A simplified scheme for small taxpayers: one flat payment covering taxes, pension and health insurance. The more generous it is, the more people leave the informal economy.
An annual tax on personal wealth. The richest pay it, but it also pushes savings out of the country or into hiding.
Funding for national universities, free and open to all. An Argentine tradition that brings hundreds of thousands onto the streets whenever it is cut.
Grants and salaries for researchers in the national science system. It keeps talent at home and produces technology in the long run.
The strategy on the sovereignty claim over the Malvinas/Falklands, South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands: rallying the country behind the cause or prioritising relations with the great powers.
How open the economy is: tariffs, the bloc with Brazil and the agreement with the European Union. Farmers gain from opening up; protected industry does not.
Replace the peso with the US dollar. It ends money printing and inflation at the root, but the country loses monetary policy and the central bank needs dollars it does not have.
Bars anyone with a corruption conviction upheld on appeal from running for office.
Deployment of federal forces, criminal intelligence and control of the Paraná river ports, with the city of Rosario at its centre.
One-off payments to pensioners, welfare recipients and informal workers to get through a crisis. Very popular, very expensive and often paid for by printing money.

The dollar floats between a floor and a ceiling adjusted for inflation. If it hits the ceiling, the central bank sells reserves to defend it. The harder the band is defended, the steadier the dollar, but the more reserves burn.
High rates keep savers in pesos and hold down the dollar and inflation, but make credit expensive, cool the economy and choke indebted small businesses.
Drastic cuts to transfers, public works, state salaries and subsidies to eliminate the deficit. It brings down inflation and wins market confidence, but people feel the squeeze.
A legal commitment not to spend more than is collected: every new outlay needs a cut or a tax. It anchors expectations, but forces the government to veto popular laws.

Sale or concession of the national airline, water utility, airport services, freight railways and other state firms. It brings in dollars and shrinks the deficit, but meets union and nationalist resistance.
Hundreds of rules repealed by decree: rents, private health plans, retail, aviation. It frees competition and investment, but leaves many sectors unprotected.

column3: Delegated powers and rule by decree
column4: Congress hands legislative powers to the executive, which governs through emergency decrees. It is fast, but erodes institutions and angers the opposition.
A close alliance with Washington: a US Treasury swap line, a trade agreement and support at the IMF. It props up the peso, but strains ties with China and part of the electorate.
Non-contributory pensions and payments to care providers, transport and therapy centres for disabled people. Cutting them saves money, but triggers protests from families and providers.
Funding and salaries for national referral hospitals such as the Garrahan children's hospital. If they are starved of funds, specialists leave and conflicts erupt.
Inspections of laboratories and medicines. If they are relaxed to cut red tape, contaminated products may slip through.

Lets people spend undeclared savings without explaining their origin and presumes taxpayers innocent. It could bring billions in hidden savings into the economy, but opens the door to money laundering.
An amnesty to declare unregistered dollars and assets for a small levy. It raises revenue and adds deposits, but rewards those who evaded.
The income tax paid by higher-earning employees. Restoring it raises a lot, but angers powerful unions such as truckers, bank workers and oil workers.
Raises for national government employees: civil servants, university lecturers, national hospital doctors and the security forces.
A per-child allowance and a food-purchase card for the poorest families. It is the main safety net against child destitution.
Roads, housing, sewers and dams funded by the national government. It creates jobs and connects the provinces, but it is expensive and historically a source of graft.

Dissolving or shrinking agencies such as the national roads authority or the agricultural and industrial technology institutes. It saves money and cuts red tape, but loses technical capacity the private sector does not replace.
Compulsory open primaries for all parties. They sort out the candidates, but are costly and mean one more trip to the polls.
Allows minors to be tried from age 14. Popular on the security agenda, criticised by experts and child-rights bodies.
Protection of glaciers and periglacial zones from mining. Mining provinces want it relaxed to attract copper and gold investment.
An international concession to dredge and mark the Paraná-Paraguay waterway, which carries 80% of farm exports.
